concepts.title: G.S. Ghurye: Indology and the Study of Caste
concepts.definition: G.S. Ghurye, father of Indian sociology, drew on Sanskritic textual sources -- the Indological approach -- to study Indian society, and his classic work on caste identified six features: segmental division, hierarchy, restrictions on feeding and social intercourse, civil and religious disabilities, lack of unrestricted choice of occupation, and endogamy.
concepts.key_idea: Read the classics, count the features -- Ghurye systematised caste as six linked restrictions rooted in Brahmanical texts.

explain endogamy and restrictions on feeding as caste features

solution_steps.explain: Ghurye treated Sanskrit texts and historical sources as data -- the indological route into Indian institutions.
Segmental division by birth-groups, hierarchy of rank, food and contact restrictions, civil and religious disabilities, hereditary occupation, and endogamy together mark caste.
Texts give the ideal order; critics note field reality -- and non-textual voices -- may diverge sharply from scripture.

concepts.title: D.P. Mukerji and the Tradition-Directed Path
concepts.definition: D.P. Mukerji argued Indian sociology must be grounded in the living traditions of Indian society and in proficiency with Indian languages, not merely in western concepts. Tradition, for him, was not dead custom but a dynamic inheritance; the sociologist's task was to study how tradition adapts and changes under modern forces.
concepts.key_idea: Know your own traditions and languages before theorising India -- sociology here must grow from native ground.
concepts.textbook_ref: kesy205.txt lines 160-280 (d p mukerji, tradition and modernity, importance of indian languages, dialectical approach to tradition, critique of blind westernisation)
question_patterns: why did d p mukerji stress the study of tradition

what makes a sociology of india genuinely indian

solution_steps.explain: Mukerji demanded command of Indian traditions and languages -- concepts must meet the society's own categories.
Traditions are living, contradictory and changing; they carry both vitality to draw on and rigidities to criticise.
Copying western modernity wholesale would uproot analysis; the path is critical engagement of tradition with modern forces.

worked_examples.q: Which sociologist argued Indian sociology must grow from living traditions and Indian languages: D.P. Mukerji or A.R. Desai?

concepts.title: A.R. Desai and the Marxist Approach; M.N. Srinivas and Sanskritisation
concepts.definition: Two further currents shaped Indian sociology. A.R. Desai applied a Marxist framework, reading Indian history and nationalism in terms of economic structures and class forces. M.N. Srinivas, through intensive fieldwork, gave sociology concepts from within: sanskritisation -- lower groups adopting customs of higher groups -- and westernisation, plus the village study tradition.
concepts.key_idea: Class analysis from above, village fieldwork from within -- Desai and Srinivas set the poles of Indian sociological debate.

solution_steps.explain: Desai explained institutions and movements -- including nationalism -- through changing economic structures and class interests.
Sanskritisation names the upward emulation of upper-caste customs; westernisation the adoption of western ways; the dominant caste holds local land, numbers and status.
Desai's structural analysis and Srinivas's village fieldwork display the breadth of Indian sociological practice -- macro theory and micro observation.

worked_examples.q: Which sociologist applied a Marxist framework to Indian history: A.R. Desai or M.N. Srinivas?

worked_examples.question_pattern: Two families of different castes in a village will not dine together, and marriage between them is unthinkable. Point out which of Ghurye's caste features appear in this episode.

solution_template.explain: Refusal of commensality -- eating together -- is Ghurye's restriction on feeding and social intercourse.
Unthinkable intermarriage is endogamy, the strongest boundary marker of caste in his list.
Who may eat with whom and who may marry whom encodes rank -- segmental division and hierarchy standing behind the episode.

worked_examples.question_pattern: A newly prosperous caste group abandons meat-eating, adopts vegetarian rituals and claims a sacred thread. Analyse the phenomenon using Srinivas's concept.

solution_template.explain: Emulating the customs, rituals and life-style of twice-born castes is precisely sanskritisation.
New economic prosperity seeks social recognition -- status mobility expressed through cultural imitation.
Sanskritisation changes customs more than power; critics stress it leaves the caste hierarchy itself intact.
